territory: Scheduled jobs, retention, telemetry writes: /api/retention/sweep, /api/demo/reset, src/lib/{retention,account-purge,last-seen,login-attempt,search-log,content-view,audit,auth-tokens,timing-safe,storage(delete path)}.ts, scripts/ops/{snapshot,prune}.mjs, .github/workflows/{retention,snapshot,backup}.yml, plus the schema-level cascade graph those jobs traverse

findings.title: Purging any user who is a Group creator cascade-deletes the whole group, everyone's posts in it, and the entire Catch-up (all rounds, prompts, entries) attached to it
findings.expected: Deleting one member (self-requested purge after the 60-day grace, adminDeleteUser, or adminMergeUsers of a duplicate) removes THAT member's data. Shared containers they happened to create survive, the way Catchup.createdById is SetNull precisely so 'the Catch-up survives if they leave' (schema.prisma:702).
findings.actual: Group.creatorId is `onDelete: Cascade` (schema.prisma:201: `creator User @relation(fields: [creatorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)`). `prisma.user.delete` inside purgeUserAccount therefore deletes every Group the member created, which cascades: Post.groupId Cascade (schema.prisma:406) deletes every OTHER member's posts in the group; Catchup.groupId Cascade (schema.prisma:717) deletes the Catch-up, then CatchupEdition -> CatchupPrompt -> CatchupEntry -> CatchupEntryLove all Cascade, destroying every member's answers. Two creation paths make this near-certain to fire: (1) signup auto-creates 'Batch of {year}' groups with `creatorId: userId` for whoever signs up first from a batch — the code itself says the creator exists 'only to satisfy the required FK' (src/components/auth/actions.ts:212-227); (2) starting a Catch-up sets `creatorId` on its private group (catchups/actions.ts:446). None of the three deletion paths handles createdGroups: purgeUserAccount only clears filed reports then `prisma.user.delete` (account-purge.ts:99-102); adminDeleteUser delegates to it (admin-actions.ts:59); adminMergeUsers re-points posts/comments/photos/entries but never groups, then deletes the source (admin/people/actions.ts — no occurrence of 'group' in the file), so merging a duplicate can also destroy a batch group while the just-re-pointed posts die with it. The retention sweep runs this UNATTENDED (retention.ts:121), so 60 days after the first-of-their-batch member requests deletion, their entire batch group and every classmate's group posts and catch-up history silently vanish overnight. Additionally, the cascaded rows of OTHER authors carry R2 image URLs (Post.images, CatchupEntry.images) that nothing deletes — collectImageUrls only reads the purged user's own rows (account-purge.ts:38-46) — so those bytes are orphaned in R2 forever on top of the row loss.
findings.evidence: schema.prisma:201 `creator  User          @relation(fields: [creatorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)`; schema.prisma:406 `group       Group?       @relation(fields: [groupId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)` on Post; schema.prisma:717 `group     Group            @relation(fields: [groupId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)` on Catchup, whose editions/prompts/entries are all Cascade (744, 764-765, 784-786). auth/actions.ts:220-227: `if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({ data: { name, description: ..., visibility: "public", creatorId: userId } ... }` with the comment 'they become its creator only to satisfy the required FK'. account-purge.ts:99-102: `await prisma.$transaction([ prisma.report.deleteMany({ where: { reporterId: userId } }), prisma.user.delete({ where: { id: userId } }) ]);` — no group handling. retention.ts:120-121 runs it nightly per due account. The schema's own SetNull on Catchup.createdById ('nullable so the Catch-up survives if they leave', schema.prisma:702) proves the survival intent that the Group cascade defeats.
findings.fixDirection: Break the ownership cascade: make Group.creatorId nullable with onDelete: SetNull (matching Catchup.createdById), via a dated file in prisma/migrations-manual/ (ALTER the FK constraint + DROP NOT NULL), plus `npx prisma generate`. Audit the few readers of group.creatorId for null-handling. Alternatively (weaker) purgeUserAccount/adminMergeUsers could re-point or explicitly guard createdGroups before user.delete, but SetNull at the schema level is the only version that protects every future delete path. Decide separately whether a purged sole-member private group should be garbage-collected deliberately rather than by FK accident.
findings.gateOrTest: New unit/integration test: create user A, have A's signup mint a batch group, add user B with a post in it and a catch-up entry; purge A; assert the group, B's post, and B's entry all survive. Pin in src/lib/security-regressions.test.mjs style, plus a schema assertion that Group.creatorId is not Cascade.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (proving it live would destroy real shared rows in the ONE shared database; the cascade chain is fully visible in schema.prisma)

findings.title: Account purge deletes DB rows first and R2 bytes best-effort afterwards with the URL list held only in memory: any failure, crash or timeout mid-loop orphans the member's images in R2 permanently, while the audit entry claims they were removed
findings.expected: A purge (GDPR Art. 17, audits H9/M35) reliably removes the member's R2 objects, or at minimum leaves a durable record of what still needs removing so a retry can finish the job; the audit trail reports what actually happened.
findings.actual: purgeUserAccount collects URLs in a local array, deletes the rows in a transaction, then loops `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; }` (account-purge.ts:109-112). Three defects compound: (1) delImageByKey swallows every error (`catch { /* best-effort cleanup */ }`, storage.ts:225-227), so a transient R2 429/500 during the loop silently skips the object — and because the pointing rows are already gone, the file's own comment admits 'afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' (account-purge.ts:79-81): the miss is permanent and the bytes stay publicly fetchable at pub-*.r2.dev, which is exactly the pre-H9 failure this module exists to close. (2) `deleted` counts loop iterations, not successes, and flows into the audit detail `${purged.imagesDeleted} stored image(s) removed` (retention.ts:132, admin-actions.ts:70), so the compliance record can state images were removed when none were. (3) If the serverless function crashes or hits its duration ceiling between the row transaction and the end of the loop (see the unbounded-sweep finding), every remaining URL is lost with the process. There is no persisted work list, no retry, and no orphan-reconciliation sweep on the R2 side.
findings.evidence: account-purge.ts:108-113: `let deleted = 0; for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; } return { ok: true, imagesDeleted: deleted };` — increment is unconditional. storage.ts:218-228: `export async function delImageByKey(key: string): Promise<void> { try { ... DeleteObjectCommand ... } catch { // best-effort cleanup } }` — void return, error swallowed, caller cannot know. account-purge.ts:77-81 comment: 'URLs are collected FIRST, because the cascade takes the pointing rows with it and afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' — i.e. the in-memory array is the last copy. retention.ts:131-132 writes `"${purged.imagesDeleted} stored image(s) removed"` into the account.purge audit row.
findings.fixDirection: Make the object list durable before the row delete: either (a) delete R2 objects keyed by prefix instead of by collected URLs — all app-minted uploads live under `uploads/<userId>/...` and `avatars/<userId>/...` (see ownedUploadUrls and the merge's avatar note in admin/people/actions.ts:322-330), so a ListObjectsV2+delete over those two prefixes AFTER the row delete is re-runnable and misses nothing even on crash; or (b) persist the collected URLs into a small PendingImagePurge table in the same transaction as user.delete, drain it in the loop, and let the nightly sweep retry leftovers. Also make delImageByKey return success/failure and count only true successes in imagesDeleted.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test with a stubbed storage layer: make delImage fail for one of three URLs, assert imagesDeleted reports 2 (not 3) and that the failed key remains discoverable (pending row or prefix listing) for a retry; a second run must remove it.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof would require deleting a real account; the swallow-and-count-anyway path is fully visible in the two quoted functions)

findings.title: Admin-message screenshots (AdminMessage.imageUrl) are never deleted from R2 by any path: account purge misses them and the retention sweep's 2-year deleteMany orphans them
findings.expected: purgeUserAccount is 'the ONE meaning of gone' (SECURITY.md): every R2 object class a member created — avatar, post images, catch-up entry images, Collection photos, admin-message screenshots — is removed at purge. And when the retention sweep expires AdminMessage rows at 730 days, the bytes those rows point at go with them.
findings.actual: AdminMessage has `imageUrl String? // one optional screenshot (WebP via /api/upload)` (schema.prisma:587), written by the member-facing messages actions (`create: { authorId: session.user.id, fromAdmin: false, body, imageUrl }`, messages/actions.ts:94). collectImageUrls queries only User.photoUrl, Post.images, Photo thumb/url/original, and CatchupEntry.images (account-purge.ts:38-46) — AdminMessage is absent, so on purge the member's screenshots (bug reports and admin conversations, which routinely contain personal data) survive in R2, publicly fetchable, with the pointing rows cascade-deleted (AdminThread.memberId Cascade -> AdminMessage.threadId Cascade) so nothing can ever find them again — the exact H9 failure mode, via a model added after H9 was closed. Independently, the sweep's `prisma.adminMessage.deleteMany({ where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff(730) } } })` (retention.ts:73-77) deletes rows without touching imageUrl bytes, so every screenshot older than two years becomes an untracked orphan on the normal nightly path too. A repo-wide grep of delImage callers (upload/finalize, collection, admin/people, feed, settings, storage, account-purge) confirms no code path anywhere deletes an AdminMessage image.
findings.evidence: account-purge.ts:37-46: `const [user, posts, photos, entries] = await Promise.all([ prisma.user.findUnique(...photoUrl...), prisma.post.findMany(...images...), prisma.photo.findMany(...), prisma.catchupEntry.findMany(...images...) ]);` — four sources, no adminMessage. retention.ts:73-77: `(await prisma.adminMessage.deleteMany({ where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff(KEEP_DAYS.adminMessages) } } })).count` — pure row delete. schema.prisma:590 `thread AdminThread @relation(fields: [threadId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)` plus schema.prisma:568 AdminThread.member Cascade completes the purge-time row cascade.
findings.fixDirection: Add `prisma.adminMessage.findMany({ where: { authorId: userId, imageUrl: { not: null } }, select: { imageUrl: true } })` to collectImageUrls (or supersede the whole collector with the uploads/<userId>/ prefix delete from the previous finding, which covers this class automatically). For the sweep, select imageUrl of the about-to-expire rows and delImage each before/after the deleteMany.
findings.gateOrTest: Extend the purge test: member sends an admin message with a screenshot; purge; assert the object is gone from storage (local-fs mode makes this assertable in a unit test). Second test for the sweep path with a backdated AdminMessage row.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (live proof would require purging a real account; the absent query in collectImageUrls is definitive)

findings.title: Visit and SearchLog have no retention mechanism at all: absent from the sweep, absent from prune.mjs, absent from the SECURITY.md retention table — Visit alone can consume the 500MB database tier within roughly a year at 2,000 members
findings.expected: Every table that grows with traffic has something bounding it (the sweep, a prune, or a by-design cap), and the owner's retention table covers all personal-data tables. The project's own standard: prune.mjs exists because one unbounded table 'can actually exhaust' the 500MB free tier.
findings.actual: runRetentionSweep deletes from exactly seven tables (adminMessages, reports, contributions, notifications, loginAttempts, auditLogs, outboundEmails — retention.ts:73-107) plus due accounts; prune.mjs touches only Notification. Nothing anywhere deletes Visit or SearchLog rows (repo-wide grep for visit/searchLog deleteMany: zero hits outside generated code; the only non-telemetry readers are admin-analytics SELECTs). Both tables were added 2026-08-19, AFTER prune.mjs was written, whose header still claims 'Nothing else here grows unbounded' (prune.mjs:9-10) — that claim is now false. Arithmetic: a Visit row is one per member-sitting and carries ~20 columns including two path strings, referrer, four geo strings, UA-derived strings and coordinates (~300-450 bytes with tuple overhead) plus three indexes (PK, endedAt, [userId,endedAt]). 2,000 members at the schema's own engagement assumption (last-seen.ts:23 uses '2,000 members at 30 views a day') is 1,500-3,000 visits/day = 0.5-1.1M rows/year, roughly 250-600MB/year — on the same 500MB Supabase free tier that prune.mjs cites, this is the largest and fastest-growing table in the schema and it is unbounded. SearchLog is smaller (60s per-user dedupe, all three scopes require auth so userId is always set) but also unbounded and additionally pays a full btree on the raw query text (@@index([query]), schema.prisma:1003). Neither table appears in the SECURITY.md retention table (docs/SECURITY.md:82-90 lists only the seven swept classes), so the published policy has no answer for how long presence/search personal data is kept — a GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) gap in exactly the framework the sweep was built to satisfy (retention.ts:6).
findings.evidence: retention.ts:23-40 KEEP_DAYS has keys only for adminMessages, reports, contributions, notifications, securityLogs, sentEmailLog — no visits, no searches. prune.mjs:5-10: 'notifications are ~0.8KB each and accumulate forever... the ONE thing in this schema that can actually exhaust it. Nothing else here grows unbounded' — written before Visit/SearchLog existed. Grep across src/ and scripts/ for `visit.deleteMany|searchLog.deleteMany|DELETE FROM "Visit"|DELETE FROM "SearchLog"`: no matches. schema.prisma:1013-1016 (ContentView comment) shows the team already did this arithmetic for views ('2,000 members at twenty views a day is 14M rows a year, which is gigabytes on a 500MB plan') and chose a bounded counter — the identical reasoning was never applied to Visit.
findings.fixDirection: Pick retention windows with the owner (e.g. Visit 90-180 days — the analytics room's questions are about recent behaviour; SearchLog 180-365 days) and add two deleteMany steps to runRetentionSweep (both tables need a createdAt/endedAt-leading index for the sweep predicate: Visit already has @@index([endedAt]); SearchLog has @@index([scope, createdAt]) which does not lead on createdAt — add @@index([createdAt]) or sweep per-scope). Record both in the SECURITY.md retention table and in the KEEP_DAYS comment block.
findings.gateOrTest: Extend the sweep's result type and any sweep test to include visits/searches counts; a schema-coverage assertion (every model with a traffic-driven insert path appears either in KEEP_DAYS, in prune.mjs, or on an explicit bounded-by-design list) would catch the next telemetry table added without a policy.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: `SELECT count(*), pg_total_relation_size('"Visit"') FROM "Visit"` via the admin analytics room or a read-only query; growth rate over a week extrapolates the arithmetic.

findings.title: Two contradictory Notification retention policies ship simultaneously: prune.mjs deletes at 30 days while retention.ts and the published SECURITY.md policy say 1 year — the effective behavior is 30 days and the sweep's notification step is dead code
findings.expected: One owner decision, one mechanism. The documented policy (SECURITY.md retention table: 'Notifications | 1 year', mirrored in retention.ts:32-33 'Notifications: 1 year. Purely transient by design') is what members experience.
findings.actual: snapshot.yml runs `node scripts/ops/prune.mjs --days 30` nightly (snapshot.yml:75), and prune.mjs's comment claims its own owner mandate: 'the owner asked for a flat 30 days' (prune.mjs:47-49). So notifications are actually destroyed at 30 days — a member returning from a two-month absence finds an empty bell, 11 months earlier than the published policy promises. Meanwhile runRetentionSweep's `notification.deleteMany({ createdAt: { lt: cutoff(365) } })` (retention.ts:88-92) can never match a row, because prune removed everything older than 30 days long before it turns 365 — the step is permanently a no-op that still reports a reassuring 0 in the nightly audit JSON. Both files cite the owner for different numbers; at least one record of his decision is wrong, and the schema comment at Notification (schema.prisma:534-536, 'the 100-per-user prune') references a third mechanism that does not exist anywhere in the codebase (no such code; grep finds only the flat-30-days prune).
findings.evidence: prune.mjs:23 `const DAYS = args.includes("--days") ? Number(...) : 30;` and :47-49 'A notification nobody opened in a month is not going to be opened; the owner asked for a flat 30 days.' vs retention.ts:32-33 `/** Notifications: 1 year. Purely transient by design. */ notifications: 365,` vs docs/SECURITY.md retention table row '| Notifications | 1 year |' captioned '(owner, 2026-08-19)'. snapshot.yml:72-75 wires prune into the nightly run.
findings.fixDirection: Ask the owner which number is the decision; then delete the losing mechanism entirely (if 30 days: remove the notifications step from KEEP_DAYS/retention.ts and fix the SECURITY.md table; if 1 year: remove the prune step from snapshot.yml or point prune.mjs at 365). Also fix the stale '100-per-user prune' comment at schema.prisma:534-536 and prune.mjs's now-false 'nothing else grows unbounded' header.
findings.gateOrTest: A one-line assertion tying the two constants together is impossible across .mjs/.ts, so pin the surviving policy in the sweep's unit test and delete the other code path; docs check in the audit-status tracker.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: `SELECT min("createdAt") FROM "Notification"` — if the oldest row is ~30 days old, prune is winning and the 1-year policy is fiction.

findings.title: Retention-sweep step failures are invisible to the nightly alarm: every step's error is caught, the route answers HTTP 200, and retention.yml only fails on HTTP status — a permanently failing account purge (a member's legal deletion request never finalising) shows green forever
findings.expected: The workflow's own design note: a failure 'fails loudly, which is the correct symptom' (retention.yml:14). A night where a table's delete or an account's purge failed should turn the GitHub run red, because that run is the only automated observer.
findings.actual: `step()` swallows every exception (`catch (err) { console.error(...); errors.push(name); return 0; }`, retention.ts:66-70) and per-account purge failures merely push `purge:${row.id}` (retention.ts:122-125); the route then returns `NextResponse.json(result)` — always 200 (route.ts:34-35). retention.yml's guard is `curl -sS -f` (retention.yml:41-45), which reacts only to the HTTP status, so a night where EVERY step failed (DB hiccup, a new FK blocking user.delete, R2 credentials rotated) still produces a green Actions run. The only trace is the errors array inside the retention.sweep audit-row JSON — and if the DB is the thing failing, that final writeAudit fails silently too (audit.ts:67-71 catches everything, logging only outside production), leaving zero trace anywhere. The console.error lines go to Vercel function logs, which nobody reads nightly and the Hobby plan retains only briefly. The worst concrete case: a deletion-requested account whose purge fails repeatedly (e.g. a future RESTRICT FK, the H8 pattern) is never erased, with a green tick every morning.
findings.evidence: retention.ts:63-71: `const step = async (name, fn) => { try { return await fn(); } catch (err) { console.error(...); errors.push(name); return 0; } };` route.ts:34-35: `const result = await runRetentionSweep(); return NextResponse.json(result);` — no status branching on result.errors. retention.yml:41-45: `# -f turns an HTTP error (401, 500) into a job failure ... curl -sS -f ...` — the mechanism exists but nothing ever produces the 500.
findings.fixDirection: Return a non-2xx (e.g. 500) from the route when `result.errors.length > 0` — the deleteMany steps are idempotent so the workflow's retry-by-rerun costs nothing — or keep 200 and have retention.yml parse the JSON body and `exit 1` on a non-empty errors array (jq is available on ubuntu-latest). Either way the audit row should still be written first.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on runRetentionSweep with one step forced to throw: assert errors non-empty; route-level test asserting the HTTP status reflects it.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (forcing a step failure against the shared production database is not acceptable)

findings.title: The sweep's account-purge loop is unbounded (findMany with no take, sequential per-URL R2 deletes) against the serverless duration ceiling: a backlog of due accounts or one photo-heavy member can kill the run mid-purge, amplifying the orphaned-bytes defect
findings.expected: A nightly job on a Vercel function bounds its work per invocation so it cannot hit the platform duration ceiling, and anything it must finish (R2 cleanup after row deletion) is not in the killable tail.
findings.actual: `prisma.user.findMany({ where: { deletionRequestedAt: { lt: cutoff(DELETION_GRACE_DAYS) } }, ... })` has no `take` (retention.ts:116-119), and each due account then runs collectImageUrls (4 queries) + a transaction + `for (const url of urls) await delImage(url)` — one sequential R2 round trip per object (account-purge.ts:109-112). A member with a large Collection contribution can alone mean hundreds of serial DeleteObject calls; several accounts falling due the same night (or accumulating behind a stretch of failed runs — see the invisible-failure finding) multiplies it. Neither the route nor vercel.json exports/configures `maxDuration` (route.ts has no segment config; vercel.json contains only regions/framework/crons), so the function runs under whatever the plan's default ceiling is (60s classic Hobby; up to 300s under Fluid) and is killed at it. Because R2 deletion happens after row deletion per account, the kill lands exactly in the window that orphans bytes permanently (see the purge-ordering finding); the run's final audit entry and result are also never written, and the GH job records a bare curl failure with no partial-result JSON. The seven deleteMany steps are single fast statements and are fine; the purge loop is the unbounded part.
findings.evidence: retention.ts:115-136: `const rows = await prisma.user.findMany({ where: { deletionRequestedAt: { lt: cutoff(DELETION_GRACE_DAYS) } }, select: {...} }); for (const row of rows) { const purged = await purgeUserAccount(row.id); ... }` — no take, no time budget. account-purge.ts:109-111: `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); ... }` — serial. vercel.json (whole file quoted in audit notes) has no functions/maxDuration block; sweep/route.ts exports only GET.
findings.fixDirection: Cap the nightly batch (`take: 10`, oldest deletionRequestedAt first) — leftovers are naturally picked up tomorrow since the predicate re-derives; export `maxDuration` explicitly on the route at the plan's maximum; batch the R2 deletes (DeleteObjects supports 1000 keys per call, or Promise.allSettled in chunks of ~10). The prefix-delete redesign from the purge-ordering finding removes the per-URL serial loop entirely.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test asserting the sweep processes at most N accounts per run; the existing sweep-idempotency reasoning (retention.ts:14-16) already covers the resume-next-night behavior.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (cannot stage a purge backlog against the shared database)

findings.title: Every fire-and-forget telemetry write (recordLoginAttempt, logSearch x3, recordView x4, the AuthToken opportunistic sweep) is a bare void'ed promise with no after()/waitUntil: on Vercel its completion after the response is not guaranteed, so login-attempt/search/view data is silently and intermittently lost
findings.expected: Work that must outlive the response on a serverless platform is registered with `after()`/`waitUntil` — the codebase itself does exactly this for the mail-queue drain ('it must run AFTER the response has been streamed', layout.tsx:58-69) — or is awaited before the response is produced.
findings.actual: recordLoginAttempt internally detaches its write (`void prisma.loginAttempt.create({...}).catch(...)`, login-attempt.ts:46-59) and is invoked from authorize() in src/lib/auth.ts at 7 call sites; the failed-login paths return to the client almost immediately after, so the create races the function freeze. logSearch is `void`-ed in two API routes immediately before `return NextResponse.json(...)` (users/search/route.ts:72-78 then :80 return; places/search/route.ts:127-134) — and logSearch is itself two sequential DB round trips (dedupe findFirst then create/update, search-log.ts:50-79), widening the race window. recordView is `void`-ed in four RSC pages that finish rendering right after. None uses `after()`. Vercel's execution model freezes the instance once the response completes; a pending promise may resume on a later invocation or never, so under real traffic some fraction of LoginAttempt/SearchLog/ContentView writes silently vanish — undermining precisely the surfaces they were built for: 'who cannot sign in' (login-attempt.ts:20-27 says an invisible locked-out member is the failure this exists to prevent) and the zero-result search list. The loss is unobservable because every one of these writers deliberately logs failures only outside production. touchLastSeen is NOT affected (awaited in the layout's Promise.all, layout.tsx:35-52). The auth-tokens.ts:107 void'ed deleteMany is the benign end of the same pattern (self-heals on next mint).
findings.evidence: login-attempt.ts:44-46: 'Deliberately not awaited by the caller...' `void prisma.loginAttempt.create({...})`. places/search/route.ts:127-135: `void logSearch({ scope: "places", ... }); return NextResponse.json(results);`. layout.tsx:63 shows the codebase's own correct pattern for post-response work: `after(async () => { ... await drainMailQueue(); ... })`. search-log.ts:50-72 shows logSearch performs findFirst + create — two awaits inside the detached promise.
findings.fixDirection: Wrap each detached call in `after(() => ...)` from next/server (route handlers and RSC pages both support it in Next 16), or simply await them — each is one-to-two fast same-region round trips and the routes already await a rateLimit check. For recordLoginAttempt, have it return the promise and register it via after() in auth.ts, or accept the await (~5ms in bom1). Keep the never-throws contract either way.
findings.gateOrTest: Grep-style regression check: no `void logSearch|void recordView` outside an after() callback (a small unit test over source text, in the spirit of security-regressions.test.mjs). Live: compare LoginAttempt row counts against Vercel function invocation counts for /login over a week.
findings.reproPlan: Live-but-safe partial proof: sign in with a wrong password on production a few times in quick succession, then count matching LoginAttempt rows in /admin (owner-visible) — a shortfall confirms drops; absence of shortfall does not disprove (timing-dependent).

findings.title: retention.yml and snapshot.yml both fire at 21:00 UTC despite retention.yml's comment claiming it avoids simultaneity: the sweep's Notification deleteMany and prune.mjs's batched Notification DELETEs run concurrently, and the night's metric counts are taken mid-sweep
findings.expected: The nightly jobs are staggered, as their own comments intend: backup 20:30 UTC, then non-overlapping successors ('inside the same quiet-hours window as the backup ... but not simultaneous with either', retention.yml:18-20; 'half an hour after backup.yml, so the two never contend', snapshot.yml:11-12).
findings.actual: Both schedules are literally `- cron: '0 21 * * *'` (retention.yml:21, snapshot.yml:16). retention.yml's 'not simultaneous with either' enumerates only backup and the catchups cron; snapshot was never added to the claim. Consequences, mild but real: (1) snapshot's collectDb counts (mail_sent, notifications-adjacent aggregates, members_total during a purge night) run while the sweep is deleting from the same tables, so the recorded history for a purge night is off by the sweep's deletions depending on statement interleaving; (2) the sweep's `notification.deleteMany` (retention.ts:88-92) and prune.mjs's loop of `DELETE FROM "Notification" WHERE id IN (SELECT ... LIMIT 5000)` (prune.mjs:63-72) target overlapping row sets concurrently on two different poolers (app transaction pooler vs DIRECT_URL session pooler) — ordinary row-lock waits, with a small deadlock surface between an unbounded single-statement delete and a batched one. GitHub's cron jitter means they usually won't start the same second, but nothing orders them.
findings.evidence: retention.yml:17-21: `schedule: # 21:00 UTC == 02:30 IST: ... but not simultaneous with either. - cron: '0 21 * * *'`. snapshot.yml:14-16: `schedule: - cron: '0 21 * * *'`. Both claim 02:30 IST in their own comments.
findings.fixDirection: Move snapshot.yml to 21:30 UTC (03:00 IST) or retention to 21:30; update both comments. (Resolving the Notification double-policy finding removes half the contention on its own.)
findings.gateOrTest: None needed beyond the cron lines themselves; a comment-accuracy fix travels with the schedule change.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (schedule facts are in the two files)

findings.title: snapshot.mjs runs at 21:00 UTC but queries PostHog for 'today's UTC date', so the 21:00-24:00 UTC window (02:30-05:30 IST) is never counted on any day — a permanent 3-hour hole in the one metrics history built to outlive the vendors
findings.expected: Each day's posthog.events/people/pageviews row eventually reflects the full day: either the job snapshots the *previous* completed day, or a later run overwrites today's partial numbers with final ones.
findings.actual: `DAY = startOfUtcToday()` (snapshot.mjs:28-33) and the HogQL filter is `WHERE toDate(timestamp) = toDate('${iso}')` with iso = DAY (snapshot.mjs:196-203). Running at 21:00 UTC, the query covers 00:00-21:00 of the current UTC day; events from 21:00-24:00 UTC are attributed to a date the job will never query again (tomorrow's run asks about tomorrow). The upsert `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` (snapshot.mjs:282-283) would heal it if a run ever re-asked about a past day, but none does. Sentry's `statsPeriod=24h` (snapshot.mjs:168) has the mirror-image quirk: a rolling window labelled with the run day, overlapping 3h of the prior day's row. Small in absolute terms (02:30-05:30 IST is deep night for an IST membership) but it is a systematic bias in the exact artifact whose stated purpose is to 'say in 2028 what the site looked like in 2026' (snapshot.mjs:7-9).
findings.evidence: snapshot.mjs:27-28: `const DAY = args.includes("--day") ? new Date(`${dayArg}T00:00:00Z`) : startOfUtcToday();` snapshot.mjs:196-203: HogQL `WHERE toDate(timestamp) = toDate('${iso}')` with `const iso = DAY.toISOString().slice(0, 10)`.
findings.fixDirection: Have the PostHog (and Sentry) collectors snapshot YESTERDAY's completed UTC day (`daysAgo(1)`) instead of today, keeping db/github collectors on 'now' semantics; or add a second small upsert for yesterday's posthog metrics in the same run. Label which metrics are point-in-time vs completed-day in the admin room.
findings.gateOrTest: A --dry run comparison across two consecutive days would show the gap; after the fix, posthog.pageviews for day N should match PostHog's own UI for day N.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only: compare a stored posthog.pageviews row against the PostHog dashboard's figure for the same date; the stored one will be consistently lower.

findings.title: snapshot.mjs --day backfill records TODAY's live database, Sentry and GitHub values under the requested past date, silently corrupting the historical series it claims to backfill
findings.expected: The workflow_dispatch input advertises 'Backfill a specific day (YYYY-MM-DD)' (snapshot.yml:19-21): running it for 2026-08-01 writes numbers that describe 2026-08-01.
findings.actual: Only the PostHog collector actually uses DAY as a data filter. collectDb computes `count(*) FROM "User"` etc. — the CURRENT totals — and its windows are `daysAgo(7)/daysAgo(30)` relative to the requested day but evaluated against present-day lastSeenAt values (snapshot.mjs:60-104); collectSentry always queries `statsPeriod=24h` from now (snapshot.mjs:168); collectGithub reads the latest backup runs (snapshot.mjs:228-241). All of these rows are then upserted under the past `day` (snapshot.mjs:277-285), overwriting whatever genuine numbers that day's original run captured. So using the advertised backfill after, say, a missed night writes today's member/post/mail totals into the missing date — and if run for a date that already has data, it destroys correct history. The header comment even acknowledges the tension ('the only source that can be asked about the past', snapshot.mjs:56-58) without acting on it.
findings.evidence: snapshot.mjs:73-104: the big SELECT has no reference to DAY except `d7/d30` lower bounds on lastSeenAt — `(SELECT count(*) FROM "User") AS members_total` is unconditionally current. snapshot.mjs:277-284: `const day = DAY.toISOString().slice(0, 10); await db.query(`INSERT INTO "MetricSnapshot" ... ON CONFLICT ("day","source","metric") DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value ...`)` — current values keyed under the past day. Also snapshot.mjs:27: `--day` with a missing/malformed value yields Invalid Date and the run fails with an unhelpful throw.
findings.fixDirection: Restrict --day to the posthog source (skip db/sentry/github collectors when backfilling, since their numbers cannot be recovered for the past), or rename/re-document the input as 'PostHog-only backfill'. Validate dayArg (exists, matches YYYY-MM-DD, produces a valid Date) before connecting.
findings.gateOrTest: A --dry --day run should list only posthog.* metrics after the fix.
findings.reproPlan: Safe live proof with --dry: `node scripts/ops/snapshot.mjs --day 2026-01-01 --dry` prints db.members.total equal to today's count under the 2026-01-01 label (writes nothing).

findings.title: snapshot.mjs backup.ok reads workflow_runs[0], which can be an in-progress or manually-dispatched run with conclusion null, recording a false backup failure for the day
findings.expected: github.backup.ok = 1 whenever the most recent COMPLETED backup succeeded; the metric exists to answer 'did last night's backup run, and did it pass' (snapshot.mjs:222-224).
findings.actual: `const last = runs[0]; add("github", "backup.ok", last?.conclusion === "success" ? 1 : 0);` (snapshot.mjs:235-236) takes the newest run regardless of status. GitHub scheduled workflows routinely start late by 10-40 minutes; backup fires at 20:30 UTC (backup.yml:34) and snapshot at 21:00, so on a night where backup's start slipped past ~20:58 (or the dump is slow), runs[0] is `in_progress` with `conclusion: null` and backup.ok is recorded 0 even though the backup then succeeds. A manual `workflow_dispatch` of backup near the snapshot time produces the same false negative, and `backup.age_hours` (snapshot.mjs:237-239) similarly uses the possibly-running run. The stored history then shows phantom backup failures that never happened.
findings.evidence: snapshot.mjs:228-241: fetches `/actions/workflows/backup.yml/runs?per_page=10` with no `status=completed` filter; `add("github", "backup.ok", last?.conclusion === "success" ? 1 : 0)`. backup.yml:34: `- cron: '30 20 * * *'`; snapshot.yml:16: `- cron: '0 21 * * *'` — a 30-minute nominal gap against GitHub's documented multi-minute cron jitter.
findings.fixDirection: Add `&status=completed` to the runs query (the API supports it), or take the first run whose conclusion is non-null. Keep failures_last_10 over completed runs only for consistency.
findings.gateOrTest: After the fix, manually dispatch backup and immediately run snapshot --dry: backup.ok must reflect the previous completed run, not 0.
findings.reproPlan: Safe live proof: trigger backup via workflow_dispatch, run `node scripts/ops/snapshot.mjs --dry` while it is in progress, observe `github.backup.ok = 0` printed despite the last completed backup having succeeded.

findings.title: After a purge, other members' User.coverPhoto (and Group.coverImage) strings still point at the purged uploader's deleted Collection photo bytes, leaving broken cover images with no cleanup or fallback path in the purge
findings.expected: When a purge deletes a contributor's Photo rows (uploaderId Cascade) and their R2 bytes, surfaces that reused those photos degrade gracefully — the referencing field is cleared or the renderer falls back.
findings.actual: User.coverPhoto is 'a Collection photo url reused as profile cover' (schema.prisma:104) — a plain string with no FK. purgeUserAccount deletes the uploader's Photo rows via the user.delete cascade (Photo.uploaderId Cascade, schema.prisma:172) and then deletes the bytes those rows pointed at (collectImageUrls gathers thumbUrl/url/originalUrl, account-purge.ts:41-44). Nothing updates other members whose coverPhoto equals one of those URLs (grep: no coverPhoto handling in account-purge.ts or admin actions), so their profiles are left requesting a now-404 object. The purge comment explicitly reasons about whose bytes they are (account-purge.ts:33-35) but not about the dangling reuse references. Whether members see a broken-image glyph or an acceptable empty state depends on the profile renderer, which is why this is 'suspected': the dangling pointer is certain, the visual severity needs one render check.
findings.evidence: account-purge.ts:33-35: '`coverPhoto` is deliberately absent: it is a Collection photo REUSED as a profile cover, so its bytes belong to whoever contributed it' — the reasoning covers whose bytes to delete, not who still points at them. schema.prisma:104: `coverPhoto String? // a Collection photo url reused as profile cover` — no relation, so no cascade or SetNull can fire.
findings.fixDirection: In purgeUserAccount, after collecting the URL set, `prisma.user.updateMany({ where: { coverPhoto: { in: urls } }, data: { coverPhoto: null } })` (and the same for Group.coverImage if groups resurface) inside the delete transaction; independently, make the cover renderer tolerate a failed image load.
findings.gateOrTest: Purge test: member B sets member A's photo as cover; purge A; assert B.coverPhoto is null (or the profile renders the no-cover state).
findings.reproPlan: Live proof possible on the demo deployment only (set a cover from a seeded photo, delete the uploader via admin, view the profile); do not run on production.

verifiedClean: 6e/CRON_SECRET handling: both cron routes (retention sweep route.ts:24-28, demo reset GET route.ts:99-103) compare `Bearer ${secret}` with timingSafeEqualStrings (crypto.timingSafeEqual with length pre-check, timing-safe.ts:12-16) and fail CLOSED when the env var is unset — examined, clean

demo/reset against the REAL deployment: POST answers 404 and GET answers a 200 no-op skip BEFORE any database or seed code runs (route.ts:62, :91); CRON_SECRET alone cannot trigger a reseed because IS_DEMO (server-only DEMO_MODE=1, demo.ts:21) short-circuits first — hard refusal confirmed, clean

6i two sweeps overlapping: retention.yml has `concurrency: group: retention / cancel-in-progress: false` serialising scheduled+dispatch runs; every deleteMany is a hard-cutoff idempotent statement (retention.ts:14-16); a concurrent duplicate purge degrades to a caught P2025 (ok:false, error entry) with no double-delete or corruption — clean

touchLastSeen (the CLAUDE.md incident): the loud-in-dev guard exists (last-seen.ts:175-184 logs when NODE_ENV !== production); the call IS awaited inside the layout's Promise.all (layout.tsx:35-52), so it is not in the fire-and-forget loss class — clean

6h IST/UTC seam in last-seen/proxy: the 15-minute lastSeenAt throttle (LAST_SEEN_STALE_MS, last-seen.ts:24,167-173) and the 30-minute visit gap (rolling cookie maxAge in proxy.ts:284-292) are pure duration arithmetic with zero calendar/day-boundary math, so a session spanning IST midnight cannot split or misattribute; retention cutoffs (retention.ts:20) are rolling Date.now() offsets, equally seam-free — examined, clean

Visit upsert race: the visit id rides an httpOnly cookie minted by the proxy, with a DERIVED (not random) fallback so parallel cold-cache requests agree (proxy.ts:257-283), the value is format-validated (/^[0-9a-z-]{8,64}$/) bounding the PK, and the upsert keys on the primary id with no read-then-write — the historical six-rows-per-sitting race is genuinely closed — clean

AuthToken growth: bounded by the opportunistic deleteMany of rows 7 days past expiry on every mint (auth-tokens.ts:101-118, backed by @@index([expiresAt])); the table cannot grow while nothing mints — clean

ContentView 'bounded by design' claim: verified — upsert on the compound unique (viewerId, kind, targetId) (content-view.ts:29-33) means one row per pair, never per view; viewer rows cascade on purge; rows for deleted targets persist by documented deliberate choice (schema.prisma:1029-1031) and drop out of analytics joins harmlessly — claim holds

Audit-log survival of purge: AuditLog has deliberately NO foreign keys (schema.prisma:494-505), the sweep captures name/email context BEFORE the delete (retention.ts:113-133), and writeAudit for account.purge uses actorId null — 'admin X deleted member Y' provably outlives Y — clean

Money survives purge: Contribution.userId is nullable with onDelete: SetNull ('a deleted account must never take the record of its money with it', schema.prisma:840-842,869), and the sweep keeps payment rows 10 years (KEEP_DAYS.contributions=3650) — clean

SearchLog write shape: all three logging surfaces (feed page, /api/users/search, /api/places/search) require a session before logging, so userId is always present and the 60-second per-(user,scope,query) dedupe applies (search-log.ts:49-70); queries are trimmed and capped at 120 chars — write-amplification clean (growth itself is the separate unbounded-retention finding)

Sweep idempotency/resumability: each step is an independent hard-cutoff deleteMany that survives sibling failures (step wrapper, retention.ts:63-71); a missed night deletes two days' worth next night; the purge list re-derives from deletionRequestedAt each run so a partial run resumes for remaining accounts — clean

collectImageUrls input handling: malformed JSON images columns are skipped per-row without failing the purge (account-purge.ts:56-66); keyForUrl refuses traversal segments and unknown roots on the delete path (storage.ts:235-262) — clean
prune.mjs mechanics: batched 5000-row deletes to keep session-pooler transactions short, --days floor of 7, --dry mode — mechanically clean (the 30-vs-365 POLICY conflict is the separate finding)

6d pgbouncer compatibility in territory: the purge uses the array form $transaction and catchup creation an interactive one — both are transaction-unit operations safe through the transaction pooler; no SET/advisory-lock/LISTEN usage anywhere in these files; snapshot/prune use the session pooler from Actions as designed — clean
6f 4.5MB body cap: no route in this territory accepts a request body (sweep and reset GET/POST are body-less) — not applicable, checked

recordLoginAttempt inputs: email trimmed/lowercased/sliced to 200 before write (login-attempt.ts:49), reasons are a closed union, no password ever passed — clean (its delivery guarantee is the fire-and-forget finding)
IS_DEMO interplay: the sweep skips entirely on the demo (route.ts:30-32) and writeAudit short-circuits on IS_DEMO (audit.ts:55), so demo noise cannot reach the real audit trail — clean
coverageNotes: Read whole: src/app/api/retention/sweep/route.ts, src/lib/retention.ts, src/lib/account-purge.ts, src/lib/last-seen.ts, src/lib/login-attempt.ts, src/lib/search-log.ts, src/lib/content-view.ts, src/lib/audit.ts, src/app/api/demo/reset/route.ts, src/lib/timing-safe.ts, scripts/ops/snapshot.mjs, scripts/ops/prune.mjs, prisma/schema.prisma (full, for the cascade walk), .github/workflows/retention.yml and snapshot.yml, src/app/(main)/layout.tsx, vercel.json. Read targeted sections: storage.ts delete path (delImage/delImageByKey/keyForUrl), auth-tokens.ts mint/sweep, proxy.ts publicPaths + visit-cookie block, docs/SECURITY.md retention section, docs/OPERATIONS.md schedule claims, backup.yml schedule line, demo.ts IS_DEMO, admin-threads-server.ts, messages/actions.ts imageUrl writers, admin/people/actions.ts merge tail, components/profile/admin-actions.ts adminDeleteUser, catchups/actions.ts creation transaction, components/auth/actions.ts joinBatchGroup, and every call site of touchLastSeen/recordLoginAttempt/logSearch/recordView (grep-driven: feed page, users/places search routes, profile/letters/collection/round pages, auth.ts call lines). The full-cascade purge walk covered every schema model with a User relation (verified onDelete per model: Cascade for content/engagement/telemetry, SetNull for Contribution/SearchLog/AdminMessage.author/Catchup.createdBy, no-FK for AuditLog/LoginAttempt/RosterEntry — the Group.creatorId Cascade being the one that breaks the intent). Consciously skipped as other investigators' territory: /api/catchups/tick internals and advanceDueCatchups (catchups territory — I read only its layout wiring), email-queue drain internals (email territory — I verified only OutboundEmail's retention bound), admin-analytics.ts query correctness (admin territory — I used it only to confirm Visit/SearchLog have no delete paths), backup.yml dump mechanics, demo-seed contents, and the uncommitted auth.ts/rate-limit.ts beyond their recordLoginAttempt integration. LoginAttempt retaining purged members' emails for 365 days was examined and deliberately NOT reported: it matches the documented 'Login + audit logs | 1 year' owner policy. The searchLog dedupe findFirst-then-create race was examined and dropped as analytics noise below the reporting bar. Live confirmation was not attempted per hard rule 1; the two 'suspected' findings carry safe repro plans.
